intro.html: Three small Latin parts run through this topic. greg means flock or herd, the way sheep crowd together. plac means please or calm, and pac means peace (you know it from Pacific, the ocean early sailors found calm).

greg = flock: gregarious people love the flock; crowds congregate (flock together); an aggregate adds everything to the flock; to segregate is to set apart from the flock; and an egregious mistake stands out from the flock. plac = please, calm, and pac = peace: placate, placid, implacable, complacent, pacify.
Watch the little prefix in front of each root: it tells you which way the flock moves, or whether the calm is there at all (im- in implacable means not).

words.def: fond of company; happiest when with other people
words.ex: Our {gregarious} neighbor knows the name of every family on the block and most of their dogs.
words.ctx: Unlike her quiet brother, who could spend a whole weekend alone with a book, Tia was {gregarious}: she planned picnics, joined three clubs and talked to everyone at the bus stop.
words.etym: From Latin gregarius, “belonging to a flock,” from grex (flock, herd).

mn.cue: GREG and his FLOCK of friends
mn.text: Wherever Greg walks, a whole flock of friends tags along, laughing and talking; a man who loves company that much is {gregarious}.

scene.alt: Greg waves as a happy crowd of friends, and even a sheep, follows him through the park.

words.def: shockingly bad; standing out for being so wrong
words.ex: Printing the wrong date on every wedding invitation was an {egregious} mistake.
words.ctx: A small spelling slip can be forgiven, but the newspaper’s error was {egregious}: it named the wrong winner of the science fair in a headline across the whole front page.
words.etym: From Latin egregius, “standing out from the flock”: e- (out of) + grex (flock). In English it first meant outstandingly good.

mn.cue: EGG-GREE-jus: eggs on the king’s rug
mn.text: The new cook trips and drops a whole crate of eggs on the king’s royal rug; a blunder that stands out that badly is {egregious}.

scene.alt: A young cook trips and spills a crate of eggs across the throne room as the king cries out.

words.def: to gather together in a crowd
words.ex: Every evening the ducks {congregate} near the bench where Granny Mae sits.
words.ctx: On hot afternoons the town’s teenagers {congregate} at the public pool; by four o’clock there is hardly room to spread a towel.

roots.means: to make, to act on (in verbs)

words.etym: From Latin congregare, “to flock together”: com- (together) + grex (flock).

mn.cue: a CONGA line at the GATE
mn.text: When the band strikes up, the whole street forms a conga line at the garden gate; when people gather in a crowd like that, they {congregate}.

labels.text: CONGA at the GATE: all GATHER

scene.alt: Neighbors dance in a conga line, all crowding together at a garden gate.

words.def: a whole made by adding many parts together; a total
words.ex: The {aggregate} of all the class’s penny jars came to almost forty dollars.
words.ctx: No single gift to the shelter was large, but the {aggregate} was impressive: hundreds of small donations added up to enough for a new roof.
words.etym: From Latin aggregare, “to add to a flock, to join”: ad- (to) + grex (flock).
words.note: As a verb (AG-rih-gayt), aggregate means to collect into one whole. “In the aggregate” means taken all together.

mn.cue: ADD the GREG (flock) through the GATE
mn.text: Farmer Lin counts the sheep from every field as they trot through one gate; the grand total of the whole flock is the {aggregate}.

scene.alt: Sheep file through a farm gate while the farmer holds up a sign with the total count.

words.def: to set apart from the rest; to keep separate
words.ex: At the recycling center, workers {segregate} glass from paper and plastic.
words.ctx: To keep the cough from spreading, the farmer had to {segregate} the sick lambs, moving them to a pen far from the healthy flock until they recovered.

roots.means: to make, to act on (in verbs)

words.etym: From Latin segregare, “to set apart from the flock”: se- (apart) + grex (flock).
words.note: In American history, segregation names the unjust laws and customs that kept people of different races apart; the civil rights movement fought to end them.

mn.cue: a SEParate GATE, apart from the flock
mn.text: The farmer leads the coughing lamb through a separate gate into its own pen until it is well; to keep it apart from the flock is to {segregate} it.

scene.alt: A farmer points a sick lamb through its own gate, away from the rest of the flock.

words.def: to calm someone’s anger, often by giving them something
words.ex: To {placate} the crying toddler, Dad offered him a ride on his shoulders.
words.ctx: The manager tried to {placate} the angry diners with free desserts, but they still grumbled about waiting an hour for their meal.

roots.means: to make, to act on (in verbs)

words.etym: From Latin placare, “to calm, to soothe,” related to placere (to please).

mn.cue: a PLAte of CAKE: calm at last
mn.text: When Grandpa Gus grumbles about the rain, Nana Lou sets a plate of cake in front of him, and the frown melts; she knows how to {placate} him.

scene.alt: A grumpy grandfather sits at a table as his wife brings him a slice of cake to cheer him up.

words.def: calm and peaceful; not easily stirred up
words.ex: At dawn the {placid} lake held the mountains like a mirror.
words.ctx: The old mare was {placid}, standing quietly through thunder and fireworks, while the young colt bolted at every bang.
words.etym: From Latin placidus, “gentle, calm,” from placere (to please).

mn.cue: a PLACE to SIT: still water
mn.text: Grandpa’s favorite place to sit is the river at sunrise, where not a ripple moves and even the duck dozes; it is {placid}.

labels.text: a PLACE to SIT: so CALM

scene.alt: An old man sits peacefully fishing by a still river while a duck dozes on the water.

words.def: impossible to calm, please or change
words.ex: The {implacable} wind howled for three days without a pause.
words.ctx: Apologies, gifts and promises all failed; the old rival remained {implacable}, refusing even to shake hands at the reunion.
words.etym: From Latin implacabilis: in- (not) + placabilis (able to be calmed).

mn.text: The children offer the roaring dragon a cake, a song and a bunch of flowers, but it roars on; it is not placate-able, it is {implacable}.

scene.alt: Two children hold out a cake and flowers to a dragon that keeps roaring angrily.

words.def: so pleased with oneself that one stops watching for danger or trying to improve
words.ex: After ten wins in a row, the team grew {complacent} and skipped practice.
words.ctx: Because the bakery had no rivals for years, its owners grew {complacent}; when a new shop opened with fresher bread, they lost half their customers in a month.
words.etym: From Latin complacere, “to please greatly”: com- (thoroughly) + placere (to please).

mn.text: The shepherd gets so comfy in his place that he naps while the sheep wander off; too pleased with himself to keep watch, he is {complacent}.

scene.alt: A shepherd dozes in his chair while his sheep stroll out of the open gate.

words.def: to calm someone down or bring peace to a place
words.ex: Rocking the cradle slowly was the only way to {pacify} the fussy baby.
words.ctx: When the two neighbors began shouting over the fallen tree, Mrs. Ruiz stepped in to {pacify} them, offering to split the cost of hauling it away.
words.etym: From Latin pacificare, “to make peace,” from pax (peace).

mn.text: A baby’s pacifier is named for what it does: pop it in, the crying stops, and peace returns. It helps {pacify} the baby.

scene.alt: A toddler sits calmly hugging a teddy bear while his mother whispers that there is peace at last.

head: word
prefix
literally
after.cap: One root, five directions: the prefix tells which way the flock moves.

after.html: Two look-alikes to keep apart: complacent means smug and too comfortable, while complaisant means eager to please others. And placid describes something already calm, while to placate or pacify is to make someone calm.

items.q: After years at the top, the champion stopped training hard and lost to a newcomer. She had become…
items.why: She was too pleased with her success to keep working: complacent. Complaisant means eager to please others.

items.q: True or false: today, calling a mistake egregious is a kind of praise.
items.why: False. Long ago egregious meant standing out from the flock in a good way, but today it means shockingly bad.
se- means apart, as in separate and secede. To segregate is to set apart from the flock (greg).

items.q: We offered the goat carrots, cabbage and even a song, but it kept butting the gate. The goat was…
items.why: Nothing could calm or satisfy it, so it was implacable (im- = not, plac = calm).

items.q: Which word describes something that is already calm, rather than an action that makes someone calm?
items.why: Placid is an adjective: a placid lake is calm. Placate and pacify are verbs for making someone calm.
